housing_supply.current_policy: Over the past decade, California has taken a lot of power over housing approvals away from cities and given it to the state. [SB 35](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB35) (2017) created a fast track for qualifying apartment projects in cities that miss their state housing targets: approval becomes "ministerial," meaning local officials must say yes if the rules are met, with no discretion to say no. [SB 423](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB423) (2023) extended that fast track to 2036 and stretched it into parts of the coast. [SB 9](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB9) (2021) made it possible to build duplexes and split lots on most single-family properties "by right" — meaning approval is automatic if you meet the rules. The state also gives each region a housing target, called a Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA). When a city's local housing plan is out of step with the law, a state rule called the Housing Accountability Act limits its power to reject housing — and [AB 1893](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB1893) (2024) put real teeth into the "Builder's Remedy," which lets developers bypass local zoning in cities that aren't meeting their housing goals.
key_facts: The current RHNA cycle (2023–2031) calls for about 2.5 million new homes statewide — roughly 1 million of them affordable to lower-income families.

[SB 9](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB9) (2021) was used far less than expected. In its first year, Los Angeles got 211 unit applications, San Francisco 25, San Diego 7, and San José just 1 — even though a 2021 Terner Center analysis had estimated about 700,000 units could become newly feasible.
Cities that don't comply with state housing-plan law can be fined $10,000 to $600,000 a month.

The [SB 35](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201720180SB35) / [SB 423](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB423) fast track only kicks in where a city is missing its housing targets or doesn't have a state-approved housing plan. SB 423 also added wage and skilled-worker requirements that scale with project size.
The Surplus Land Act requires local agencies to give affordable housing first priority when they sell off public land they no longer need.
housing_supply.comparison: California has gone further than almost any state in overriding local zoning. A few others have moved this way too — Oregon ended single-family-only zoning statewide in 2019, and Montana and Washington passed broad laws in 2023 allowing more housing on existing lots. But many states still leave land-use decisions almost entirely to cities and towns.
housing_supply.arguments_for_change: Supporters of stronger state control say local government caused a housing shortage that has lasted decades. The Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) traces the state's nation-leading rents and home prices directly to building too little near coastal job centers. Supporters argue cities cave to homeowner pressure to block new housing, so only firm state mandates — automatic "by-right" approval, enforceable targets, and the Builder's Remedy — can close the gap. They point to [SB 9](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB9) as proof that voluntary tools fall flat when cities still have room to drag their feet.
housing_supply.arguments_against_change: Opponents say land-use decisions belong with local officials, who know their own neighborhoods — the roads, the fire risk, the traffic, the character of the place. They argue statewide, one-size-fits-all mandates override plans that local voters approved, and that fast-tracked "by-right" projects can skip environmental review and public input. They also say the real causes of the shortage are high construction costs, interest rates, and a tight labor supply — not zoning — so overriding cities adds conflict without reliably producing affordable homes.

prop13_commercial.explainer: Proposition 13, passed by voters in 1978, sets how California taxes property. Your property tax is capped at 1% of what you paid for the property, and the taxable value can only go up about 2% a year — no matter how much the property's market value climbs. The full bill only comes due when the property is sold and reassessed at the new price. This applies to homes, stores, offices, and factories alike. "Split-roll" means taxing business property differently from homes; California does not currently do this.
prop13_commercial.current_policy: Under [Prop 13](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3497) (1978), all California property — homes, stores, offices, and factories — is taxed at 1% of its purchase price, and the taxable value can rise no more than 2% a year until the property is sold and reassessed. Business property gets no separate ("split-roll") treatment. [Prop 15](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=15&year=2020) (2020) would have changed that for most commercial and industrial property, taxing it at current market value while leaving homes under Prop 13's rules. It failed, 52% to 48%.
key_facts: [Prop 13](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3497) caps the property tax rate at 1% of the purchase price and limits annual growth in taxable value to 2% — until the property changes hands and is reassessed.

The LAO estimated [Prop 15](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=15&year=2020) would have raised $6.5 billion to $11.5 billion a year for local governments and schools once fully phased in (around 2025).
Of that money, roughly 60% would have gone to cities, counties, and special districts, and 40% to schools and community colleges (LAO).
Prop 15 left homes out entirely. It also exempted small businesses with $3 million or less in California commercial property, plus up to $500,000 of business equipment.
Prop 15 lost statewide, 51.9% to 48.1%, in November 2020.
prop13_commercial.comparison: California is unusual in taxing business and residential property the same way — locking both to the purchase price. Most states reassess all property toward current market value every so often. As a result, a California commercial building held for decades can be taxed far below a nearly identical one that sold recently.
prop13_commercial.arguments_for_change: Supporters of a commercial split-roll say [Prop 13](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3497)'s purchase-price rule lets long-held business property — office towers, malls, big industrial sites — be taxed on values that are decades out of date. That shifts more of the tax load onto newer owners and homeowners. They point to the LAO's $6.5–$11.5 billion estimate as steady money for schools and local services, and argue that taxing business property at market value — while still protecting homeowners and small businesses — fixes the imbalance without touching home protections.
prop13_commercial.arguments_against_change: Opponents say higher taxes on commercial property get passed down to tenants — small businesses, restaurants, renters — and ultimately to shoppers, raising prices across the economy. They warn that reassessing property at market value every year is complicated and invites lawsuits, that it would hit businesses hardest in downturns when values and rents are shaky, and that weakening Prop 13 for any kind of property opens the door to chipping away at home protections later — undoing the predictability voters voted for in 1978.

tax_top.current_policy: California's top personal income tax rate is 13.3% — the highest of any state. It applies to taxable income above roughly $1 million, and voters made it permanent through [Prop 30](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=30&year=2012) (2012) and [Prop 55](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016) (2016). On top of that, a 1% Mental Health Services Tax from [Prop 63](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=63&year=2004) (2004) applies to income over $1 million, and a 2024 change added another 1.1% on wages over $1 million to fund state disability insurance. The tax on company profits has been 8.84% (10.84% for banks) since 1997.
key_facts: Top individual rate: 13.3% — the highest in the U.S. Next closest: New York 10.9%, New Jersey 10.75%, Oregon 9.9%.
The top 1% of filers pay roughly half of all personal income tax the state collects (Legislative Analyst's Office).
The 8.84% tax on company profits is middle-of-the-pack among states that tax corporate income.
Texas, Florida, Nevada, Washington, and several other states have no state income tax at all.
Leaning so heavily on top earners makes the state's revenue progressive but unstable — it swings sharply up in good years and down in recessions.
tax_top.comparison: California's tax system is more progressive than most states', leaning hard on top earners — but that also makes its revenue more volatile. Add in federal taxes, and the highest earners face a combined top rate above 50%.
tax_top.arguments_for_change: Supporters of raising rates on top earners or companies say the wealthiest residents and most profitable corporations captured most of the state's income growth, so they can afford to pay more. They argue steady revenue is needed to avoid cutting safety-net programs, and that California can ask more of its top earners without scaring off the income they generate.
tax_top.arguments_against_change: Opponents say California already has the nation's highest top rates. They point to IRS data showing more high-income filers have moved out to no-tax states than have moved in since 2020, argue that depending on a small group of top earners makes the budget wildly unpredictable, and warn that higher taxes on company profits push more headquarters to leave the state.
